title: Fitted avatars: automatic skeleton adjustment for self-avatars in virtual reality
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of accurately fitting a self-avatar to a user's body dimensions in virtual reality, so that inverse-kinematics animation produces more realistic body posture and less visible misalignment. The authors argue that common low-cost VR setups often rely on uniform avatar scaling from height alone, which can leave the avatar's limbs, shoulders, and joints mismatched to the user and reduce embodiment.

They propose an automatic avatar-fitting framework that uses an HTC Vive HMD, two hand controllers, and three trackers on the waist and feet. Through a short sequence of guided exercises, the system estimates shoulder and neck joint locations as well as limb lengths, then performs two-pass adjustment: uniform scaling followed by skeleton tuning of the arm, leg, and spine chains. A final walk-in-avatar step lets the user align themselves to compute exact tracker-to-joint offsets for animation.

The evaluation used 27 adult participants drawn from one academic institution, including faculty/staff and master's/Ph.D. students, in an immersive VR setup. The study compared fitted avatars against uniform scaling across multiple avatar body types. Quantitative results showed significantly reduced hand and leg misalignment with the fitted method, and the perceptual study showed higher ownership and overall embodiment for avatars with proportions unlike the user's when fitted scaling was used. The authors conclude that automatic skeleton adjustment improves avatar motion accuracy and can increase perceived embodiment, although some artifacts remain and the approach depends on users correctly performing the calibration exercises.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed within-subject experimental study with statistical testing (repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t-tests) and a comparison condition, but it is not randomized in the RCT sense and has a modest sample size. It provides reasonably credible evidence, though the setting is specialized VR and not K-12 education.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention shows clear positive effects on avatar alignment and embodiment, but the impact is mostly on a technical/UX outcome rather than direct learning gains. For the requested K-12 evidence context, this is adjacent and informative but not a demonstrated educational outcome effect.

interventions.use_case: virtual self-avatar fitting and embodiment support in immersive VR, using automatic skeleton adjustment to match the user’s body dimensions and improve avatar movement fidelity

finding.finding_summary: The fitted-avatar condition improved sense of embodiment for users when the avatar body proportions differed from the participant’s. In the DA condition, paired t-tests showed significantly higher overall SoE for Fitted vs. Uniform (t=2.34, df=21, p<0.029) and higher Ownership (t=2.72, df=21, p<0.013), while Change and Agency were not reported as significantly different.
finding.measure: Embodiment questionnaire: ResizeAccuracy, Ownership, Agency, and composite SoE
finding.study_size: n=27 total; SoE t-test reported on df=21 for the DA condition

finding.finding_summary: The automatic fitting pipeline reduced avatar-tracker misalignment relative to uniform height scaling, improving setup accuracy and reducing the need for manual body measurement. Quantitatively, hand and leg alignment errors were significantly lower under the fitted method across avatar types, with reported distance improvements on the order of 2.6-14.0 cm depending on gender/avatar condition.
finding.measure: HandDist, LegDist, and knee angle during scripted movement exercises
finding.std_deviation: reported in Table 1 as means ± SD; e.g., HandDist male Uniform SA 7.54 ± 3.20, Fitted SA 0.24 ± 0.66
